lines.text: Back at the board. Name any opening to walk through it, or say what to sharpen.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to c 5 if it's still legal.
This game is the Sicilian Defense.

Their c5 fights for the center from the flank: d4, holding back your d-pawn. The rule behind e4: stake out the center and grab space with the pawn to e4, because pieces behind a strong center reach either wing in a move or two. Their knight is still on g8, so nothing hits your pawn on e4 yet — it doesn't need a guard; development comes first.
Got it — after your move, they play c takes d 4 if it's still legal.

It's the Smith-Morra Gambit of the Sicilian Defense. It offers a pawn, and they almost always take it on d4. In the main line you stay a pawn down for at least 4 moves, playing for time instead of material.
Their c-pawn takes d4 opens the c-file for the rooks.
Got it — after your move, they play d takes c 3 if it's still legal.
It's the Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted of the Sicilian Defense.
Their pawn bears down on d2, keeping your knight off it — d2 sits right beside their king.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to d 6 if it's still legal.

They play d6 first, to free their knight on b8 for knight to d7 — a piece left at home cannot join the fight, and whoever has more pieces out wins the fights when the center opens. Knight takes c3, not b-pawn takes c3, which would leave an isolated pawn on c3. Their pawn bears down on e5, holding back your e-pawn.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to c 6 if it's still legal.

Their knight bears down on d4, a square no pawn of yours can cover, and e5, holding back your e-pawn. Development first is right: their bishop is still on c8, so nothing hits your queen on d1 yet — it only needs a guard once bishop to g4 comes. Their bishop is still on c8, so nothing hits your bishop on c4 yet — it doesn't need a guard; development comes first.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to g 6 if it's still legal.

This is the Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Fianchetto Defense with your bishop to c4 and their d6 thrown in. They play g6 first, to free their bishop on f8 for bishop to g7. The knight bears down on d4, keeping their knight off it, and e5, holding back their e-pawn. Their pawn bears down on f5, backing their f-pawn's push there.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to g 7 if it's still legal.
The master games run out here, so the board sets the plan: seize the open c-file.

Their bishop to g7 wins by force: they win a pawn — it lands two moves later with bishop takes e5. Anything else, like bishop to d7, falls short. Their bishop takes aim along the long diagonal. Castle kingside follows a rule worth keeping: castle your king to safety and bring the rook toward the center — a king left in the middle gets caught the moment the center opens.
Got it — after your move, they play King takes f 7 if it's still legal.

Bishop takes f7 with check was a mistake. That took the pawn on f7, but the king on e8 takes back — you lose a bishop for a pawn. Here's how: end every move with a sweep: what of mine is undefended right now? Loose pieces are what make their tactics work — defend a loose piece or move it before it becomes their idea. You've walked into this before — loose piece, the sixth game now — the last one was against jkern1013 2 weeks ago.
They take back with king takes f7 — anything else, like king to f8, loses material in the line that follows.
Got it — after your move, they play King to e 8 if it's still legal.

After their king to e8, one move keeps you in it, and only one. Worth thinking it through. Their king steps toward safety; no place for it in the crossfire yet. Your knight to g5 with check eyes e6, a square no pawn of theirs can cover. They still have two minor pieces at home — the more they wait, the more you attack. You are down material now — the job is to make it hard: keep pieces on, since every trade makes their extra material count for more, and look for counterplay.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to f 6 if it's still legal.

Count before you take on d6: two attackers against two defenders. Not enough — start the trades there and you come out behind. Their knight bears down on d5, backing their d-pawn's push there, and e4, attacking your pawn there.
Got it — after your move, they play Queen to a 5 if it's still legal.

Your next move is not a big decision — several are about equally good, so save your time for the moves that are. Their queen bears down on d5, backing their d-pawn's push there, and e5, holding back your e-pawn. Two plans hold here — getting the queen to b4, to take the queen when it arrives there, or getting the bishop to f6, to take the knight there. They come out level, so choose the one you understand and play it with purpose.
Got it — after your move, they play Rook to f 8 if it's still legal.

Their rook to f8 stops your queen to f7, check. Anything else, like knight to h5, gives up about a point. That was the move here — it develops the queen to b3, eyeing d5, c4, e6 and f7 — f7 sits right beside their king. Their rook presses down the half-open f-file, leaning on what's left there. Their rook on f8 and bishop on g7 now stand a knight's jump apart — that is the pattern to scan for: one square your knight can reach hits both.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to g 4 if it's still legal.

Danger — a whole piece is at stake: your bishop on f4 is the only defender of your knight on g5 — and it can be taken. Remember — removing the guard takes away the piece defending a key square, and what it protected falls. It is attacked once and nothing guards it: rook takes f4 — they win a bishop.

After their knight to g4, exactly two moves limit the damage — the rest concede. Their knight bears down on e3, keeping your bishop off it, e5, holding back your e-pawn, f2, attacking your pawn there, and h2, attacking your pawn there.
Got it — after your move, they play Queen to b 4 if it's still legal.

This move hands them a tactic: they play bishop takes c3 and, three moves later, they play rook takes f4, and it wins them a rook, a bishop and a knight for a queen. You've walked into this before — walking into a tactic, the third game now — the last one was against vribak about a month ago. Rook to d5 was a mistake — it let them win material, starting with bishop takes c3. The line starts with bishop takes c3, and they win a rook, a bishop and a knight for a queen.
Your bishop on f4 is still hanging — nothing guards it yet.

There is something to collect, but your bishop on f4 is loose and under fire — secure it first; the capture will still be there. Your knight has a fork waiting on c7 — it would hit their king on e8 and rook on a8. Find the way there.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to e 5 if it's still legal.
Threat met. Your bishop steps out of the attack with bishop to g3.
Not urgent yet, but see it coming — their queen on b4 pins your knight on c3 against your rook on e1. If your knight moves, your rook on e1 is open to their queen.

The timing of bishop to g3 matters — a move earlier, their queen would have taken on g5 and won your knight. Bishop to g3 unpins your pawn on e4 — and the bishop eyes the pawn on d6. Their bishop bears down on d4, a square no pawn of yours can cover, and f4, holding back your f-pawn.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop takes g 3 if it's still legal.
Their bishop bears down on e5, holding back your e-pawn, f2, attacking your pawn there, f4, holding back your f-pawn, and h2, attacking your pawn there. Why not knight takes f8?
Got it — after your move, they play Rook takes f 2 if it's still legal.
Knight takes f8 would not have worked: it grabs the rook on f8, but bishop takes f2 with check refutes it.

That is the move this position asks for — it takes back the bishop. Their rook takes the open f-file — a highway straight into your position. How do you find a plan? First the forcing scan — checks, captures, threats. Then three things: where is their weakness, which of your pieces is worst, where is your pawn break? So the plan: get your pawn on b2 out of danger first; put a rook on the open c-file; pile up on their pawn on g6. Why that target? No pawn can ever protect it, so it needs pieces to guard it — and those pieces are tied to it.
Got it — after your move, they play Queen takes b 3 if it's still legal.
Before your move, checks, captures, threats: your pawn on b2 could be taken. Their weakness was the isolated pawn on g6. You improved your worst piece, the rook on d5, with no open file yet.

Careful — this costs a pawn if you ignore it: your pawn on b2 is the only defender of your knight on c3 — and it can be taken. It is attacked twice and nothing guards it: rook takes b2 — they win a pawn.

Their queen takes b3 stops your rook takes g4, which would hit their pawn on g6. Anything else, like queen to d4, gives up a little. Their bishop on c8 is tied down now: you hit the knight on g4 once and it is guarded once — the bishop is the guard that holds it. That is what pressure buys — a piece that cannot leave. Why not rook takes g4?
Got it — after your move, they play Rook takes b 2 if it's still legal.
Rook takes g4 would not have worked: it grabs the knight on g4, but queen takes b2 refutes it.

That's the price of a-pawn takes b3: no pawn of yours can cover b5 again, and their knight on c6 is two moves from it; from there it would hit your knight on c3. Keeping b5 guarded is part of this structure from here.

Their rook takes b2 is imprecise. Rook to f7 was their move — it would attack the knight on h7. You found it — it takes back the queen. Their rook trains on the pawn on b3 — pressure they have to answer.
Got it — after your move, they play King to f 7 if it's still legal.
Careful — your rook on g6 hangs: nothing guards it, so taking it costs them nothing.

Rook takes d6? Then they answer e-pawn takes d6 — you give up a rook for a pawn. Knight to f8? Then they answer king takes f8 — they win a knight. Their king trains on the rook on g6 — pressure they have to answer. Your passed pawn on g3 is a trump, but their knight blockades it — challenge or dislodge that blockader before it can run.
Got it — after your move, they play Rook to f 2 if it's still legal.
Threat met. Your rook steps out of the attack with rook to g5.

Rook to g5 — now rook to b1 doesn't work: the rook would just be taken on b1. Anything else, like rook takes d6, gives up a little. That move does the job here — it saves it from their king on f7, and from g5 it hits their knight on g4. Notice what their rook gave up by going to f2: your pawn on b3 isn't attacked any more, so the move you owed it is free again.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to d 7 if it's still legal.

Their bishop to d7 is a mistake — it throws away about two points of advantage. C-knight to e5 was their move — it would park a piece on e5, where none of your pawns can attack it. That gives you a way back into the game — look for it. The knight bears down on e7, attacking their pawn there, f4, keeping their rook off it, and f6, keeping their knight off it. Don't park a piece on e3 — it's the first stop for your knight on d5 on the way to h4.
Got it — after your move, they play Rook takes g 2, check if it's still legal.
Careful — their bishop on d7 hits your rook on g4, and a guard does not help: the bishop is worth less than your rook.

That wins a knight: you play rook takes g4, they answer bishop takes g4 and you play king takes f2. Their rook takes g2 with check forces the king to react, seizing the initiative for a move. The position has turned sharp — one move here is far better than the rest, so calculate before you move.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop takes g 4 if it's still legal.

They play bishop takes g4 — they win a rook. Anything else, like rook to h8, gives up five points or more. That was the move here — it takes back the rook. Their bishop bears down on f3, a square no pawn of yours can cover, and h3, a square no pawn of yours can cover.
Got it — after your move, they play King to g 8 if it's still legal.
They are hitting your knight on h7, and nothing guards it — it is lost unless it moves or gets a guard.

Their king to g8 is a mistake — it throws away more than a point of advantage. King to g6 was their move — it would attack the knight on h7. That brings you level — look for the move that does it. Their king trains on the knight on h7 — pressure they have to answer. Your rook to f1 with check takes the open f-file, where the rook belongs.
Got it — after your move, they play e takes f 6 if it's still legal.
The natural alternative, king to g7, fails: they play king to g7 and you answer knight takes g4 — you win a bishop. That is the move this position asks for — it checks the king on g8.
Got it — after your move, they play King to f 8 if it's still legal.
Their bishop has nothing defending it — find it, and taking it costs you nothing back. Before you take, check what taking it allows.

You found it — it forks the king on g8 and the bishop on g4. Their king marches up — in the endgame it stops hiding and becomes a fighting piece. Their king on f8 is hiding behind your own knight on f6 — it's on your rook's f-file. Move the knight off the line and it's check. Things have got concrete — only one move really works here; find it before anything else.
Got it — after your move, they play King to e 7 if it's still legal.

That move does the job here — it wins the bishop on g4. Their king to e7 steps off f8 so the rook can come to f8. Here is what you build toward: the outpost on f5 — no pawn of theirs can chase a piece off it. A rook-and-minor ending is won slowly: keep the pieces active and pile on the weakest pawn.
Got it — after your move, they play King to f 7 if it's still legal.

Their king trains on the knight on f6 — pressure they have to answer. Your knight to f6 lands on the f6 outpost, a square none of their pawns can attack — a piece no pawn can chase stays there for the whole game.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to d 4 if it's still legal.

Watch e3 — a knight lands there in 2 and forks your king on g2 and rook on f1, so take the square away before it arrives. Their knight trains on the pawn on b3 — pressure they have to answer. Your g4 pushes your passed pawn — passed pawns must be pushed. After the pawn to g4, f4 is weak for good, and their knight on d4 gets there in two — that square is theirs now.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight takes b 3 if it's still legal.

Their knight bears down on c5, a square no pawn of yours can cover, and d4, a square no pawn of yours can cover. Before the king moves, count the checks it walks into on each square. After the pawn to g5, h5 is weak for good, but their knight needs four moves to get there — an eternity, so don't worry about it.
Got it — after your move, they play King to g 7 if it's still legal.

Give your knight on d5 a second guard — it is your best piece, and one defender is one capture away from losing it. Knight to d5 with check forces the king to react, seizing the initiative for a move. Their plan is taking shape: the outpost on c5 — no pawn of yours can chase a piece off it.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to c 5 if it's still legal.

Their knight trains on the pawn on e4 — pressure they have to answer. The rook trains on the pawn on d6 — pressure they have to answer. There it is — their knight on c5. That was their plan: the outpost on c5.
Got it — after your move, they play Rook to f 8 if it's still legal.
Their rook to f8 prepares knight to e6, to hit your pawn on g5.
Got it — after your move, they play King takes f 8 if it's still legal.

Here is what they are after: pushing their passed pawn on the a-file — every push brings it closer to promotion. A good trade — their rook on f8 was the piece doing the most work for them, and it cost you your least useful piece. A knight ending plays much like a pawn ending — king activity and the passed pawn decide it.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to a 5 if it's still legal.
g6 — now king to f7 doesn't work: your pawn on g6 covers f7. Their pawn takes b4 away from your knight on d5. Their passed pawn is on a5 now — four squares from queening.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to b 3 if it's still legal.

Knight to c3 — now b5 doesn't work: the pawn would just be lost on b5. Watch where their moves are going — the g-file — a rook on an open file reaches your camp. Your knight on c3 is safe there, since nothing of theirs can hit it, and it has somewhere useful to go next. Your knight to c3 eyes d5 and b5, squares no pawn of theirs can cover. What's the priority here?

The priority was their pawn on d6 — it's isolated — no pawn beside it can defend it.

Their knight to d4 does two jobs: it stops your knight to b5, and it prepares b5. Their knight bears down on f3, a square no pawn of yours can cover. They have given up on pushing their passed pawn on the a-file.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to e 6, check if it's still legal.
Their knight to e6 with check forces the king to react, seizing the initiative for a move.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to f 4 if it's still legal.

Their knight bears down on d3, a square no pawn of yours can cover, d5, backing their d-pawn's push there, e6, a square no pawn of yours can cover, and g6, attacking your pawn there. The king trains on the knight on e6 — pressure they have to answer.
Got it — after your move, they play King to g 8 if it's still legal.

The natural alternative, king to e8, fails: they play king to e8 and, three moves later, you play queen takes f4 — you win a knight. g7 with check forces the king to react, seizing the initiative for a move. Their king trains on the pawn on g7 — pressure they have to answer. The plan changes here — now it's to win their weak pawn on d6. Here's how: plant your knight on d5, in front of it, so it can never advance; then bring your king and pieces to it and trade off its defenders — each one is a piece of theirs tied to it. Count it: nothing of theirs guards it — the first attacker you bring wins it. Why it matters: no pawn of theirs can protect their pawn on d6, so every piece that guards it is a piece doing nothing else.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to h 5, check if it's still legal.

Their knight to h5 with check forces the king to react, seizing the initiative for a move. Your plan from here: the d-file — a rook on an open file reaches their camp. Your knight to b5 lands on the b5 outpost, a square none of their pawns can attack. On h5 their knight touches only four squares; in the centre it would touch eight. A knight is worth the squares it reaches.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to a 4 if it's still legal.
Careful — your pawn on g7 guards your king, and they hit it twice — it falls unless you cover it. Nothing guards one of their pieces — whatever takes it is not taken back.

That was the move here — it attacks the knight on h5. That's two times now they've left a piece loose under your attack — they don't check what their move leaves behind. After every move of theirs, look first for what they left loose.
Got it — after your move, they play King to h 7 if it's still legal.

Their king to h7 is a blunder — they could have won your pawn on g7, and it is still hanging — see to it. King takes g7 was their move — it would win a pawn. That wins a knight for a pawn: you play king takes h5 and they answer king takes g7. You could take on d6 right now, but the threat is stronger than carrying it out — the material will keep, so keep it hanging over them and improve first. Pieces against bare pawns — the pawns are the only counterplay, so stop the most advanced one first; then king and pieces together finish it.
Got it — after your move, they play King takes g 8 if it's still legal.
After their king taking on g8, one move keeps the win, and only one. A piece for two pawns — you are a pawn up overall.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to d 5 if it's still legal.

King to g6 — now king to f8 doesn't work. Anything else, like king to g4, gives up five points or more. Their d5 stakes a claim in the center and opens lines for the pieces. After their pawn to d5, two moves keep the win. The rest give it away. Their pawn moved from d6 to d5, so it is no longer the weak pawn you were besieging. That plan is off. The new plan is to win their weak pawn on d5. Here's how: plant your knight on d4, in front of it, so it can never advance; then bring your king and pieces to it and trade off its defenders — each one is a piece of theirs tied to it. Count it: you hit it once and nothing of theirs guards it. Why it matters: no pawn of theirs can protect their pawn on d5, so every piece that guards it is a piece doing nothing else.
Got it — after your move, they play King to h 8 if it's still legal.

Got it — after your move, they play King to g 8 if it's still legal.
There's a forced mate here — mate in 2.

There's a mate in one here.
Checkmate — you win. That's the whole game, opening to mate. The queen on d8 checks the king on f8; e7, e8, f7, g7 and g8 are covered.
